text: The ReAct pattern combines reasoning and acting in a loop: the model thinks, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until it has enough information to answer. In this repo it's implemented as Tier 1 using langchain.agents.create_agent, the default framework choice for a single agent with tools.

react-agent is the one fully-implemented reference pattern every other pattern's package layout copies: pyproject.toml shape, src/ layout, Dockerfile, and entry point. Its tools (calculator, lookup_glossary_term) are deliberately small and dependency-free.

Routing is a workflow, not an agent: the set of possible routes is fixed in code ahead of time, and a classifier picks among predefined categories rather than inventing new ones at runtime. routing-agent demonstrates task routing, classifying a support ticket into general, refund, or technical and dispatching to a category-specific handler prompt.

Prompt chaining is a workflow where a fixed sequence of steps runs in order: outline, gate check, draft, and polish. A gate check can fail fast on a malformed or too-thin outline before it ever reaches the drafting step, avoiding wasted generation on bad input.

Parallelization demonstrates two flavors: sectioning, where an incident report is split into independent subtasks (summarize, assess severity, extract action items) that run concurrently and are aggregated programmatically; and voting, where the same prompt runs n times in parallel and a deterministic node picks the majority verdict.

Orchestrator-workers is a boundary case between workflow and agent: orchestrate, run workers, then synthesize is a fixed high-level shape, but the number and nature of the middle stage's subtasks is decided by an LLM orchestrator at runtime rather than fixed in code. Reach for it when you need multiple perspectives on a task but can't predict in advance which perspectives matter.

Evaluator-optimizer runs a generate/evaluate loop: a generator produces a response, a separate evaluator LLM call grades it against explicit criteria, and the loop repeats with feedback until the evaluator approves or a maximum iteration count is reached, whichever comes first. This differs from Self-Refine, where a single model would critique its own output instead of using two separate roles.

Map-reduce fixes what each worker does (a single prompt) but lets how many workers run vary at runtime, one per item in an input list, using LangGraph's Send API for dynamic fan-out. Aggregation of the workers' results back into a summary is programmatic, not a second model call.

In the supervisor pattern, a top-level agent delegates to specialist sub-agents through tool calls and always keeps ownership of the final reply; sub-agents never talk to the user directly and never see each other. This repo's supervisor-agent composes langchain.agents.create_agent twice rather than depending on the langgraph-supervisor package, since that library's own README now recommends the direct tool-calling approach instead.

Swarm, or handoffs, is the direct disambiguator from supervisor: when one agent hands off to a peer, control moves to that specialist entirely, and it owns the rest of the conversation. swarm-agent uses langgraph-swarm's create_handoff_tool and create_swarm directly, and the swarm remembers which agent was last active so a follow-up message in the same thread resumes with that same specialist.

Network, or mesh, is a many-to-many topology where any agent can decide which peer to call next, with no fixed hierarchy and no designated entry-point-owns-the-conversation agent. Its origin traces to AutoGen rather than a LangGraph-original idea, and of the multi-agent topologies in this repo it's the only one without a dedicated, actively-maintained first-party doc page.

Basic RAG is the simplest retrieval-augmented generation pattern: on every query, retrieve the most relevant chunks from an already-indexed collection and hand them to the LLM as context before it answers. It covers only single-pass retrieval plus generation, not query rewriting, iterative retrieval, re-ranking, or agentic decisions about whether to retrieve at all.

Retrieval k trades off completeness against noise: too low a k misses relevant context, while too high a k floods the prompt with irrelevant chunks that dilute the model's attention and drive up token cost. The embedding model used at query time must match the one used to populate the collection, or similarity scores become meaningless.

Retrieve and rerank over-fetches a wider candidate set at retrieval time, then narrows it down using a cross-encoder reranker before handing the top results to the model. This trades extra compute for better relevance ranking than a single vector similarity search alone can provide.

Corrective RAG, or CRAG, grades retrieved documents for relevance and falls back to a web search plus query rewrite when the retrieved context isn't good enough, instead of blindly trusting whatever the vector store returned. It's implemented as a cyclic, branching LangGraph StateGraph rather than a straight-line pipeline.

Self-RAG extends corrective RAG's graph with post-generation checks: a hallucination grader and an answer grader that can trigger a retry loop if the generated answer isn't actually supported by the retrieved context or doesn't address the question.

Query decomposition splits a complex question into simpler sub-questions before retrieval, either sequentially, where each sub-answer informs the next sub-question, or in parallel, where independent sub-questions are answered concurrently and then combined.

Adaptive RAG is the agentic member of the RAG series: an LLM router decides the retrieval strategy before any retrieval happens, for example choosing between the vector store and a web search, or in a more advanced form choosing among no retrieval, single-step retrieval, and multi-step retrieval.

The RAG adoption strategy doc maps every pattern in the series onto a three-tier retrieval architecture: 2-Step RAG (basic-rag, retrieve-rerank), Hybrid RAG (corrective RAG, self-RAG, query decomposition), and Agentic RAG (adaptive RAG), and gives a diagnostic order for adopting them as retrieval quality problems show up.

This repo's framework tiering starts every new pattern at Tier 1, langchain.agents.create_agent, the default single-agent ReAct loop, and only moves up with a concrete reason: Tier 2 is raw LangGraph for multiple cooperating agents or control flow a single ReAct loop can't express, and Tier 3 is deepagents for long-horizon, planning-heavy work with a virtual filesystem.

Every agent calls its chat model through agents_common.models.get_chat_model, which points at a named route on a self-hosted MLflow AI Gateway rather than holding a provider API key directly. The only credential this repo needs is MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN, which authenticates tracking, evaluation, and gateway model calls alike.
